doc.title: Eiji Kitamura interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999

title: Studying literature, then classical clarinet lessons after age 50
summary: He studied Japanese literature, not music, and at 52 took classical clarinet lessons on embouchure, tone and high notes.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: I understand you went to a university — did you study music in the university?
In Japanese I studied Japanese literature.
Japanese — only Japanese history and literature. Not music.

And every time I thought about my music, I should have taken it, music. But when I was over 50 years I found a very good teacher of clarinet. But that teacher is a classic teacher. But I need classic, basically clarinet playing, and then I began 52 years old.

Technique and how to play clarinet. Only music, very basically. And then basically technique and how to hit notes, and then it was very good for me because I couldn’t play high note hits before. But now I can play very high notes, the highest, C and C sharp, D. Very easy to play.
What did this teacher show you to make that happen?

He taught me embouchure for clarinet and how to fit reed and mouthpiece, he taught me. And he taught me the other things. Each woodwind instrument must need good tone, he said. And I learned Mozart, Bach, and many other classic music. It’s very good for me.
